title: How holograms can transform entertainment
subtitle: Technology that brings live three-dimensional images, changing shows, games and cinema
excerpt: Holograms are arriving on stage, in games and on the big screen, creating three-dimensional experiences that transform how audiences consume entertainment.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
Holograms are poised to change how audiences experience entertainment, delivering three‑dimensional images that appear to float in midair. The technology, once confined to laboratory experiments, is now appearing on stages, in gaming rooms and cinemas, promising experiences that go beyond the traditional screen.

Holograms in live shows

On stages, projecting three‑dimensional figures allows artists to disappear and reappear, creating visual narratives impossible to achieve with physical scenery. The audience sees musicians, dancers or ghostly characters occupying the same space as the performers, generating a sense of presence that intensifies emotional connection. This possibility opens doors for shows that blend human performance with digital representations, reducing the need for large lighting rigs and special‑effects setups that require lengthy assembly.

Beyond aesthetics, holographic technology enables the integration of sensors that capture audience movements, adjusting lighting and effects in real time. This interactivity creates a visual feedback loop, where the crowd’s energy shapes the performance itself, making each show unique.

Interactive games with three‑dimensional projections

In gaming environments, holograms turn the room into a battlefield or a strategy board, with elements appearing around the players. Without the need for headsets or portable screens, the action takes place in real space, requiring the user to move and interact physically. This shift alters immersion dynamics, as the barrier between the virtual and real worlds disappears, making entertainment more active and social.

In competitions, hologram projection eliminates the need for individual screens, allowing teams to compete in arenas where the setting adapts to the game. The sensation of being inside the virtual environment heightens competitiveness and opens new possibilities for e‑sports narratives.

Immersive cinema without screens

Traditional cinema relies on a flat screen that defines the visual experience. With holograms, a story can be told around the viewer, who becomes part of the scene. Characters can walk through the audience, objects float around, and light effects spread throughout the space, creating a sense of being inside the narrative. This new storytelling approach expands the director’s role, who now choreographs movements in three dimensions, and gives the audience a sense of protagonism never before seen.

To complement the visuals, three‑dimensional sound accompanies the holograms, distributing frequencies so the listener perceives the origin of audio effects. This combination of sight and hearing reinforces immersion, turning cinema into a complete sensory experience.

Economic and production impacts

Adopting holograms reduces costs associated with physical sets, complex lighting, and the logistics of transporting bulky equipment. Productions can reuse digital projections, adapting them quickly for different shows or films. Moreover, the technology allows artists who no longer perform live—such as deceased singers—to return to the stage respectfully, expanding programming options and attracting new audiences.

Brands leverage the ability to display products holographically to create advertising campaigns that stand out at live events. Consumers can interact with the digital representation, virtually testing features before deciding to purchase, increasing engagement and conversion.

Adoption challenges and the future of the experience

While the benefits are clear, implementing holograms still faces technical hurdles, such as the need for controlled environments to ensure projection quality. It also requires training professionals who can seamlessly integrate digital content into physical space. As manufacturers refine projection devices and costs drop, the expectation is that holograms will become a standard tool in events, theme parks and even education, democratizing access to immersive experiences.

From an environmental perspective, replacing physical sets with digital projections reduces material consumption and waste. Moreover, the flexibility of holograms promotes inclusion, as size and contrast adjustments can be made quickly to meet diverse sensory needs.

With the consolidation of holographic projection, Brazilian entertainment gains a tool that blends creativity, technology and sustainability, promising to transform parties, games and cinema halls into spaces where imagination takes visible form.
